questions.label: Easy
body: An arithmetic sequence satisfies u<sub>5</sub> = 18 and u<sub>12</sub> = 46. Find u<sub>30</sub>.
solution:
(7)d = 28, so d = 4 and u1 = 2.
Hence u30 = 2 + 29(4) = 118.

Hence u40 = -1 + 39(3/2) = 115/2.

questions.label: Easy
body: A geometric series has first term 12 and common ratio 1/3. Show that it converges and find its sum to infinity.
solution:
Since |r| = 1/3 < 1, the series converges.
S∞ = a/(1-r) = 12/(1-(1/3)) = 18.

body: A geometric series has first term 7 and common ratio -1/2. Show that it converges and find its sum to infinity.
solution:
Since |r| = 1/2 < 1, the series converges.
S∞ = a/(1-r) = 7/(1-(-1/2)) = 14/3.

questions.label: Medium

S∞ = a/(1-r) = 5/2/(1-(3/5)) = 25/4.

questions.label: Hard

solution:
Since |r| = 2/3 < 1, the series converges.
S∞ = a/(1-r) = 18/(1-(-2/3)) = 54/5.

questions.label: Easy
body: Prove by mathematical induction that 7<sup>n</sup> - 1 is divisible by 6 for the relevant positive integers n.
solution:
Verify the claim at the first relevant integer. Assume it is true at n=k, so the bracketed expression is a multiple of the stated divisor.
At the next relevant value, 7k+1-1 = 7(7k-1)+6, which is again a multiple of that divisor. Therefore the claim follows by induction.

questions.label: Medium
body: Prove by mathematical induction that 3<sup>2n</sup> - 1 is divisible by 8 for the relevant positive integers n.
solution:
Verify the claim at the first relevant integer. Assume it is true at n=k, so the bracketed expression is a multiple of the stated divisor.
At the next relevant value, 32k+2-1 = 9(32k-1)+8, which is again a multiple of that divisor.
Therefore the claim follows by induction.

questions.label: Medium
body: Prove by mathematical induction that 5<sup>n</sup> + 3 is divisible by 4 for odd n for the relevant positive integers n.
solution:
Verify the claim at the first relevant integer. Assume it is true at n=k, so the bracketed expression is a multiple of the stated divisor.
At the next relevant value, 5k+2+3 = 25(5k+3)-72, which is again a multiple of that divisor.
Therefore the claim follows by induction.

questions.label: Hard
body: Prove by mathematical induction that 2<sup>3n</sup> - 1 is divisible by 7 for the relevant positive integers n.
solution:
Verify the claim at the first relevant integer. Assume it is true at n=k, so the bracketed expression is a multiple of the stated divisor.
At the next relevant value, 23k+3-1 = 8(23k-1)+7, which is again a multiple of that divisor.
Therefore the claim follows by induction.

questions.label: Easy
body: Use mathematical induction to prove 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 for n ∈ ℤ<sup>+</sup>.
solution: The statement is true for n=1. Assume it holds for n=k. Add the (k+1)th term to the assumed expression and simplify to (k+1)(k+2)/2, which is the required formula with n=k+1. Hence the result follows by induction.

questions.label: Medium
body: Use mathematical induction to prove 1² + 2² + ... + n² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 for n ∈ ℤ<sup>+</sup>.
solution: The statement is true for n=1. Assume it holds for n=k. Add the (k+1)th term to the assumed expression and simplify to (k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)/6, which is the required formula with n=k+1. Hence the result follows by induction.

questions.label: Medium
body: Use mathematical induction to prove 1·2 + 2·3 + ... + n(n+1) = n(n+1)(n+2)/3 for n ∈ ℤ<sup>+</sup>.
solution: The statement is true for n=1. Assume it holds for n=k. Add the (k+1)th term to the assumed expression and simplify to (k+1)(k+2)(k+3)/3, which is the required formula with n=k+1. Hence the result follows by induction.

questions.label: Hard
body: Use mathematical induction to prove 1 + 3 + ... + (2n-1) = n² for n ∈ ℤ<sup>+</sup>.
solution: The statement is true for n=1. Assume it holds for n=k. Add the (k+1)th term to the assumed expression and simplify to (k+1)², which is the required formula with n=k+1. Hence the result follows by induction.

questions.label: Easy
body: Find the coefficient of x<sup>4</sup> in (1 + 2x)<sup>9</sup>.
solution:
The required term is C(9,4)(2x)4.
Coefficient = 126(2)4 = 2016.

solution:
The required term is C(8,5)(-3x)5.
Coefficient = 56(-3)5 = -13608.

solution:

Coefficient = 120(-2)7 = -15360.

questions.label: Easy
body: Expand (1+x)<sup>1/2</sup> up to and including the x<sup>2</sup> term, and state the interval of convergence.
solution:
Using (1+u)α = 1 + αu + α(α-1)u²/2 + ..., the expansion is 1 + x/2 - x²/8 + O(x³).
It is valid for |x| < 1.

questions.label: Medium
body: Expand (1+x)<sup>-1</sup> up to and including the x<sup>2</sup> term, and state the interval of convergence.
solution:
Using (1+u)α = 1 + αu + α(α-1)u²/2 + ..., the expansion is 1 - x + x² + O(x³).
It is valid for |x| < 1.

questions.label: Medium
body: Expand (1+2x)<sup>-1/2</sup> up to and including the x<sup>2</sup> term, and state the interval of convergence.
solution:
Using (1+u)α = 1 + αu + α(α-1)u²/2 + ..., the expansion is 1 - x + 3x²/2 + O(x³).
It is valid for |x| < 1/2.

questions.label: Hard
body: Expand (1-3x)<sup>2/3</sup> up to and including the x<sup>2</sup> term, and state the interval of convergence.
solution:
Using (1+u)α = 1 + αu + α(α-1)u²/2 + ..., the expansion is 1 - 2x - x² + O(x³).
It is valid for |x| < 1/3.

solution:
Expand using i²=-1; for a quotient multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate when needed.
The simplified result is 11-10i.

questions.label: Easy
body: For z = 1+i, find |z| and the principal argument arg(z). Hence write z in modulus-argument form.
solution:
Use |z|=√(a²+b²) and select the argument from the correct quadrant.
|z|=√2, arg(z)=π/4, so z = √2(cos(π/4)+i sin(π/4)).

questions.label: Medium
body: For z = -√3+i, find |z| and the principal argument arg(z). Hence write z in modulus-argument form.
solution:
Use |z|=√(a²+b²) and select the argument from the correct quadrant.
|z|=2, arg(z)=5π/6, so z = 2(cos(5π/6)+i sin(5π/6)).

questions.label: Medium
body: For z = -2-2i, find |z| and the principal argument arg(z). Hence write z in modulus-argument form.
solution:
Use |z|=√(a²+b²) and select the argument from the correct quadrant.
|z|=2√2, arg(z)=-3π/4, so z = 2√2(cos(-3π/4)+i sin(-3π/4)).

questions.label: Easy
body: Use de Moivre's theorem to evaluate [2(cos(π/6)+i sin(π/6))]⁴ exactly in Cartesian form.
solution:
Raise the modulus to the power and multiply the argument by the power:
8(cos(2π/3)+i sin(2π/3)) = -4+4√3i.

questions.label: Medium
body: Use de Moivre's theorem to evaluate [√2(cos(π/4)+i sin(π/4))]⁶ exactly in Cartesian form.
solution:

questions.label: Medium

solution:
Raise the modulus to the power and multiply the argument by the power:
27(cos(2π)+i sin(2π)) = 27.

questions.label: Hard

solution:

questions.label: Easy
body: A polynomial with real coefficients is P(x)=x³-8x²+29x-52. Given that 2+3i is a root, find all remaining roots.
solution:
Non-real roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs, so the conjugate of 2+3i is also a root. Factor out the associated quadratic and divide P(x).
The remaining roots are 2-3i and 4.

questions.label: Medium
body: A polynomial with real coefficients is P(x)=x³+x²+4x+4. Given that 2i is a root, find all remaining roots.
solution:
Non-real roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs, so the conjugate of 2i is also a root.
Factor out the associated quadratic and divide P(x).
The remaining roots are -2i and -1.

questions.label: Medium
body: A polynomial with real coefficients is P(x)=x⁴-2x³+6x²-8x+8. Given that 1+i is a root, find all remaining roots.
solution:
Non-real roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs, so the conjugate of 1+i is also a root. Factor out the associated quadratic and divide P(x).
The remaining roots are 1-i, 2i and -2i.

questions.label: Hard
body: A polynomial with real coefficients is P(x)=x³-7x²+15x-25. Given that 1+2i is a root, find all remaining roots.
solution:
Non-real roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs, so the conjugate of 1+2i is also a root. Factor out the associated quadratic and divide P(x).
The remaining roots are 1-2i and 5.

questions.label: Easy

solution:
Write the appropriate partial-fraction form, clear denominators and compare coefficients (or substitute convenient roots).
The decomposition is 2/(x+1)+1/(x+2).

questions.label: Medium
body: Decompose (5x-1)/((x-1)(x+3)) into partial fractions.
solution:
Write the appropriate partial-fraction form, clear denominators and compare coefficients (or substitute convenient roots).

solution:
Write the appropriate partial-fraction form, clear denominators and compare coefficients (or substitute convenient roots).
The decomposition is 4/x+(-2x+3)/(x²+1).

questions.label: Hard

solution:
Write the appropriate partial-fraction form, clear denominators and compare coefficients (or substitute convenient roots).
The decomposition is 1/[2(x+1)]+1/[2(x-1)]+1/(x-1)².

questions.label: Easy
body: Given f(x)=2x-3, g(x)=x²+1, find (f∘g)(x) and (g∘f)(x), stating any necessary domain restrictions.
solution:
Substitute the output of the inner function into the outer function.
f(g(x))=2x²-1 and g(f(x))=4x²-12x+10. Exclude values making a denominator zero or a square-root argument negative.

questions.label: Medium
body: Given f(x)=1/(x-1), g(x)=x+2, find (f∘g)(x) and (g∘f)(x), stating any necessary domain restrictions.
solution:
Substitute the output of the inner function into the outer function.
f(g(x))=1/(x+1) and g(f(x))=(2x-1)/(x-1). Exclude values making a denominator zero or a square-root argument negative.

questions.label: Medium
body: Given f(x)=x²-4, g(x)=3x, find (f∘g)(x) and (g∘f)(x), stating any necessary domain restrictions.
solution:
Substitute the output of the inner function into the outer function.
f(g(x))=9x²-4 and g(f(x))=3x²-12. Exclude values making a denominator zero or a square-root argument negative.

questions.label: Hard
body: Given f(x)=√(x+1), g(x)=x², find (f∘g)(x) and (g∘f)(x), stating any necessary domain restrictions.
solution:
Substitute the output of the inner function into the outer function.
f(g(x))=√(x²+1) and g(f(x))=x+1. Exclude values making a denominator zero or a square-root argument negative.

questions.label: Easy
body: Determine whether f(x)=x⁴-3x²+2 is even, odd or neither. Justify algebraically.
solution: Replace x by -x and simplify. Here f(-x)=f(x), so the function is even.

questions.label: Medium
body: Determine whether f(x)=x³/(x²+1) is even, odd or neither. Justify algebraically.
solution: Replace x by -x and simplify. Here f(-x)=-f(x), so the function is odd.

questions.label: Medium
body: Determine whether f(x)=x³+x is even, odd or neither. Justify algebraically.
solution: Replace x by -x and simplify. Here f(-x)=-f(x), so the function is odd.

questions.label: Hard
body: Determine whether f(x)=x²+x is even, odd or neither. Justify algebraically.
solution: Replace x by -x and simplify. Here f(-x)=x²-x, which is neither f(x) nor -f(x), so the function is neither.

questions.label: Easy
body: Describe a valid sequence of transformations taking y=f(x) to y=-2f(3x-6)+4.
solution: A valid description is: horizontal compression factor 1/3; translate 2 right; reflect in x-axis and stretch vertically by 2; translate 4 up.

questions.label: Medium
body: Describe a valid sequence of transformations taking y=f(x) to y=f((x+4)/2)-3.
solution: A valid description is: horizontal stretch factor 2; translate 4 left; translate 3 down.

questions.label: Medium
body: Describe a valid sequence of transformations taking y=f(x) to y=3-f(-x).
solution: A valid description is: reflect in y-axis; reflect in x-axis; translate 3 up.

questions.label: Hard
body: Describe a valid sequence of transformations taking y=f(x) to y=(1/2)f(2-x)+5.
solution: A valid description is: reflect in y-axis and translate 2 right; vertical scale factor 1/2; translate 5 up.

questions.label: Easy
body: Given that x-1 is a factor of x³-4x²-x+4, factorize the polynomial completely over the reals.
solution:
Divide by the given factor, then factor the resulting quadratic (or polynomial).
x³-4x²-x+4 = (x-1)(x+1)(x-4).

questions.label: Medium

2x³+x²-8x-4 = (2x+1)(x-2)(x+2).

questions.label: Medium

x⁴-5x²+4 = (x-1)(x+1)(x-2)(x+2).

questions.label: Easy
body: Find the remainder when P(x)=x³-2x+5 is divided by x - 2.
solution: By the remainder theorem the remainder is P(2). Direct substitution gives 9.

questions.label: Medium
body: Find the remainder when P(x)=2x⁴-x²+3 is divided by x + 1.
solution: By the remainder theorem the remainder is P(-1). Direct substitution gives 4.

questions.label: Medium
body: Find the remainder when P(x)=x⁵+3x²-7 is divided by x - 1.

questions.label: Hard

questions.label: Easy
body: Analyse f(x)=(2x+1)/(x-3): identify discontinuities and asymptotes, and find the axis intercepts.
solution:
Factor or divide first. The discontinuity information is x=3; the end-behaviour asymptote is y=2.
The intercepts are (-1/2,0), (0,-1/3).

questions.label: Medium
body: Analyse f(x)=(x²-4)/(x-2): identify discontinuities and asymptotes, and find the axis intercepts.
solution:
Factor or divide first. The discontinuity information is x=2 is a removable hole; the end-behaviour asymptote is y=x+2 except at x=2.
The intercepts are (-2,0), (0,2).

questions.label: Medium
body: Analyse f(x)=(3x-6)/(x+1): identify discontinuities and asymptotes, and find the axis intercepts.
solution:
Factor or divide first. The discontinuity information is x=-1; the end-behaviour asymptote is y=3.
The intercepts are (2,0), (0,-6).

questions.label: Hard
body: Analyse f(x)=(x²+1)/(x-1): identify discontinuities and asymptotes, and find the axis intercepts.
solution:
Factor or divide first. The discontinuity information is x=1; the end-behaviour asymptote is oblique y=x+1.
The intercepts are no real x-intercept; (0,-1).

questions.label: Easy
body: For f(x)=(x-2)²+1, use the restriction x≥2. Find the inverse and state its domain.
solution:
Set y=f(x), solve for x and choose the branch compatible with the restriction.
f⁻¹(x)=2+√(x-1), x≥1.

questions.label: Medium
body: For f(x)=x²+4x+7, use the restriction x≤-2. Find the inverse and state its domain.
solution:
Set y=f(x), solve for x and choose the branch compatible with the restriction.
f⁻¹(x)=-2-√(x-3), x≥3.

questions.label: Medium
body: For f(x)=3-x², use the restriction x≥0. Find the inverse and state its domain.
solution:
Set y=f(x), solve for x and choose the branch compatible with the restriction.
f⁻¹(x)=√(3-x), x≤3.

questions.label: Hard

solution:
Set y=f(x), solve for x and choose the branch compatible with the restriction.
f⁻¹(x)=x-1, x≥2.

questions.label: Easy
body: For f(x)=x²-4, describe the key features needed to sketch y=1/f(x).
solution: Zeros of f give vertical asymptotes; large |x| gives the horizontal behaviour. The key features are vertical asymptotes x=±2; horizontal asymptote y=0; y-intercept -1/4.

questions.label: Medium
body: For f(x)=x²+1, describe the key features needed to sketch y=1/f(x).
solution: Zeros of f give vertical asymptotes; large |x| gives the horizontal behaviour. The key features are no vertical asymptote; horizontal y=0; maximum (0,1).

questions.label: Medium
body: For f(x)=x(x-3), describe the key features needed to sketch y=1/f(x).
solution: Zeros of f give vertical asymptotes; large |x| gives the horizontal behaviour. The key features are vertical asymptotes x=0,3; horizontal y=0; no axis intercepts.

questions.label: Hard
body: For f(x)=(x-1)², describe the key features needed to sketch y=1/f(x).
solution: Zeros of f give vertical asymptotes; large |x| gives the horizontal behaviour. The key features are vertical asymptote x=1; horizontal y=0; y-intercept 1.

questions.label: Easy
body: Solve x³-4x=x exactly and interpret the solutions as graph intersections.
solution:
Rearrange, factor or split modulus cases as appropriate.

body: Differentiate y=x²e<sup>x</sup>, simplifying the result.
solution:
Apply the product, quotient or logarithmic differentiation rule as appropriate.
y'=eˣ(x²+2x).

questions.label: Medium
body: Differentiate y=ln x/x, simplifying the result.
solution:
Apply the product, quotient or logarithmic differentiation rule as appropriate.

questions.label: Medium

solution:

questions.label: Easy
body: Given x²+y²=25, find dy/dx.
solution:
Differentiate both sides with respect to x, remembering that y is a function of x, then collect dy/dx terms.
dy/dx=-x/y.

questions.label: Medium
body: Given x²y+y³=4, find dy/dx.
solution:
Differentiate both sides with respect to x, remembering that y is a function of x, then collect dy/dx terms.

Differentiate both sides with respect to x, remembering that y is a function of x, then collect dy/dx terms.
dy/dx=(1-yeˣʸ)/(xeˣʸ-1).

questions.label: Hard
body: Given x³+y³=6xy, find dy/dx.
solution:
Differentiate both sides with respect to x, remembering that y is a function of x, then collect dy/dx terms.
dy/dx=(2y-x²)/(y²-2x).

solution:
Use dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

solution:

questions.label: Easy
body: For f(x)=x³-3x², find and classify all stationary points and identify points of inflection where requested.
solution: Solve f'(x)=0, use sign changes or f'' for classification, and solve f''(x)=0 with a concavity check. stationary at (0,0) max and (2,-4) min; inflection at (1,-2).

questions.label: Medium
body: For f(x)=x⁴-4x², find and classify all stationary points and identify points of inflection where requested.
solution: Solve f'(x)=0, use sign changes or f'' for classification, and solve f''(x)=0 with a concavity check. stationary at (0,0) max and (±√2,-4) minima; inflections x=±√(2/3).

questions.label: Medium
body: For f(x)=x³-6x, find and classify all stationary points and identify points of inflection where requested.
solution: Solve f'(x)=0, use sign changes or f'' for classification, and solve f''(x)=0 with a concavity check. stationary at x=±√2; inflection (0,0).

questions.label: Hard
body: For f(x)=x/(x²+1), find and classify all stationary points and identify points of inflection where requested.
solution: Solve f'(x)=0, use sign changes or f'' for classification, and solve f''(x)=0 with a concavity check. stationary at x=±1; max (1,1/2), min (-1,-1/2).

howTo: HL Paper 1 rewards fluency, proof and exact reasoning. Attempt questions on separate paper without a calculator. Start with one four-question skill set, then combine topics into timed mixed sets. Mark only after finishing the whole set and redo every missed question after 48 hours.

steps.text: Complete four consecutive questions from one subtopic.
Combine one question from each topic into a 25-35 mark set.
Use roughly 1.1 minutes per mark when working under exam conditions.
Classify every error as concept, algebra, notation, proof or time pressure.

format: For the current AA HL course, Paper 1 is a 2 hour non-technology examination containing compulsory short-response and extended-response questions. A clean formula booklet is permitted. This resource is a question bank, not a predicted examination paper.
syllabus: Aligned to the Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches syllabus first assessed in 2021 and used for examinations through 2028.
disclaimer: Independent educational resource. Not endorsed by or affiliated with the International Baccalaureate Organization. All questions and solutions are newly authored.
note: This independent bank follows the five-topic structure and non-calculator Paper 1 format described in the International Baccalaureate Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches subject brief (first assessment 2021). A revised course begins with first assessment in 2029.
